phonemes.desc: Akkadian /mar/ — the first syllable of the conventional reading, identical to the Sumerogram AMAR ('calf, young animal').
Akkadian /duk/ — the second element, from the sun-god name UTU/Šamaš; the whole name means 'calf of the sun'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'mar-DOOK' — stress the second syllable; the final vowel is short in the everyday transliteration, though some scholars posit an original long /uː/.

kin.label: Akkadian
kin.form: 𒀭𒀫𒌓 (dAMAR.UTU), 'calf of the sun' — the logographic spelling used in Babylonian texts

kin.label: Sumerogram
kin.form: AMAR.UTU — AMAR = calf, UTU = the sun god Šamaš; the name is a theophoric compound

kin.label: Conventional
kin.form: Marduk — the standard Assyriological transliteration adopted into English and most modern languages

pronunciation.note: Marduk is Tier 2: the canonical Unicode restoration is the plain Latin form Marduk, which preserves no diacritic, long-vowel mark, or distinctive non-ASCII letter. A scholarly variant Mardūk with a final macron is sometimes used to mark a posited long vowel, but PuniCodex follows the lexicon's attested conventional form. The tier classification therefore reflects the name's ASCII-canonicality, not its religious or mythological importance.

domains.title: MARDUK — King of Babylon, Builder of the Cosmos
domains.subtitle: Creation, Divine Kingship, Storms, Justice
domains.lead:
Marduk began as a local storm-god of Babylon and rose, by the first millennium BCE, to become the supreme head of the Mesopotamian pantheon. His name, written 𒀭𒀫𒌓 (dAMAR.UTU), means 'calf of the sun' — a theophoric compound that binds the young animal to the solar god Šamaš. In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Marduk defeats the primordial sea Tiamat, splits her body to fashion heaven and earth, and receives from the assembled gods the kingship of the cosmos. This temple treats him as the paradigm of legitimate sovereignty: the deity who turns chaos into order by decree, combat, and architecture.

His city, Babylon, was both a political capital and a theological statement. Its ziggurat Etemenanki ('Temple of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth') and its temple complex Esagila were understood as the axis where Marduk's cosmic order touched the ground. Kings from Hammurabi to Nebuchadnezzar II ruled by his mandate, and the king's first duty was to maintain Marduk's cult. Justice, law, and the measured world were therefore extensions of his domain.

cards.name: The Winged Sun-Disc
cards.desc: The solar emblem of divine kingship; Marduk's name binds him to the sun-god Šamaš, and the winged disc proclaims celestial authority.

cards.name: Esagila & Etemenanki
cards.desc: The 'House of the Raised Head' and the ziggurat 'Foundation of Heaven and Earth' — the architectural center of Marduk's cosmic rule.

cards.name: The Four Winds
cards.desc: Marduk holds the four winds as weapons and messengers; in the Enuma Elish they are the first instruments he fashions for the storm-battle.

cards.name: The Measured Cosmos
cards.desc: After defeating Tiamat, Marduk divides her corpse into halves, sets up constellations as heavenly regulators, and establishes the calendar.

symbols.name: Winged sun-disc
symbols.meaning: The emblem of solar kingship and Marduk's link to the sun-god Šamaš

symbols.name: Spade or triangular hoe (šaruḫu)
symbols.meaning: Marduk's primary attribute, the tool with which he shapes land and clears the primordial waters

symbols.name: Mušḫuššu dragon
symbols.meaning: The snake-dragon hybrid that serves as Marduk's sacred animal, seen on the Ishtar Gate

symbols.name: Four winds
symbols.meaning: The winds Marduk deploys as weapons and messengers in the chaos-battle

symbols.name: Ziggurat / cosmic mountain
symbols.meaning: Etemenanki as the axis between heaven and earth, the material form of Marduk's ordered cosmos

mythology.lead: Marduk's mythology is the mythology of cosmic sovereignty. It is not enough for him to be powerful; he must be chosen by the gods, prove himself in combat, build the world, and then receive the legal instrument of kingship. His stories are therefore political theology in narrative form: they explain why Babylon, and by extension its god, stands at the center of the world.

myths.title: Marduk Slays Tiamat and Builds the World
myths.text: In the Babylonian Enuma Elish ('When on High'), the younger gods disturb the primordial Apsu and Tiamat. After Apsu is killed, Tiamat raises an army of monsters to avenge him. Marduk alone accepts the challenge, on condition that the gods grant him supreme kingship. He rides into battle in a storm-chariot drawn by four fearful creatures, surrounds Tiamat with the four winds, and splits her body with his bow and mace. From one half he makes the sky; from the other, the earth. He fixes the stars, the moon, and the calendar, then creates humankind from the blood of the slain god Kingu to serve the gods. The poem is both creation myth and charter for Marduk's cult in Babylon.

myths.title: Marduk Receives His Names
myths.text: The seventh and final tablet of the Enuma Elish lists Marduk's fifty names, each explained as a function or title he has absorbed from older gods. Anu, Enlil, and Ea yield aspects of their sovereignty to him; his names declare him creator, provider, judge, and shepherd. This is not mere praise but theological consolidation: by naming, the older pantheon legally transfers cosmic authority to Babylon's patron deity. The list preserves the names of deities who might otherwise have been forgotten, making the tablet a kind of annotated divine genealogy.

myths.title: Marduk and the Gift of Kingship
myths.text: The prologue to the Code of Hammurabi names Marduk as the god who called Hammurabi 'to bring about the welfare of the people' and 'to cause justice to prevail in the land.' Kingship is thus a delegated office: the king rules because Marduk has chosen him, and his laws are legitimate because they extend Marduk's own ordering power. Nebuchadnezzar II later boasted of rebuilding Esagila and Etemenanki, framing his reign as an act of cultic service to Marduk.

myths.title: Marduk's Absence and the Fall of Babylon
myths.text: The Erra Epic tells how Marduk abandons his shrine and the divine statue is desecrated, allowing the war-god Erra to devastate Babylon. When Marduk returns and his statue is refurbished, order is restored. The myth dramatizes a Mesopotamian theological anxiety: even the king of the gods can be absent, and the stability of the cosmos depends on the proper maintenance of his cult. It also reflects historical catastrophes such as the sack of Babylon by Sennacherib in 689 BCE and its later restoration under Esarhaddon.

lore.syncretism: Marduk absorbed functions from Enlil (kingship and the decree of destinies), Ea/Enki (wisdom and water), and Šamaš (justice and solar radiance). His rise parallels the political rise of Babylon: when Babylon was small, he was a local storm-god; when Babylon became an imperial capital, he became king of the gods. The Greeks identified him with Zeus Belos (Bel = Baal = 'Lord'), and Berossus transmitted Marduk-Bel to the Hellenistic world as the civic god of Babylon. In Jewish and early Christian exegesis, the figure of Bel and the dragon (Daniel 14) preserves a polemical memory of Marduk's cult statue and animal. No later deity exactly reproduces Marduk's combination of storm-combat, cosmic architecture, and urban kingship.
lore.culturalLegacy: Marduk's most visible survival is architectural: the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, now in the Pergamon Museum, is glazed in the deep lapis-blue and gold associated with his city, and its processional way is lined with mušḫuššu dragons and aurochs. The tower of Babel narrative in Genesis 11 almost certainly reflects the memory of Etemenanki. In modern fantasy and games, Marduk appears as a dragon-slaying storm-god and as the namesake of Babylonian magic. The name still means: the sovereign who turns chaos into a city.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Marduk is the god of the city as cosmos. Where Enlil rules the wind and Ea rules the sweetwater deep, Marduk rules the assembly that decides what order is. His power is not merely physical; it is constitutional. The gods vote him kingship, name him into authority, and then witness his exercise of it. This is Mesopotamian political theory rendered as myth: legitimacy comes not from strength alone but from a recognized procedure, a public mandate, and the capacity to deliver the goods — in this case, a habitable world.

To name Marduk is to remember that creation is not a single event but an ongoing administrative project. The cosmos must be maintained: the calendar kept, the temple repaired, the king watchful, the law enforced. The Enuma Elish does not end with the making of the world; it ends with the establishment of the cult that sustains it. Every ziggurat is a promise that chaos has been defeated once and can be defeated again, provided the proper rites continue. The plain Latin spelling of his name — Marduk, Tier 2 — is itself a kind of stability: no diacritic to argue over, no reconstruction to dispute, just the conventional form by which two and a half millennia of readers have known the king of Babylon.
